questions.question: Khanya Ltd: net profit after tax R450 000, net profit before tax R620 000, interest on loans R80 000, average shareholders' equity R3 000 000, average capital employed R4 000 000, one million shares, total dividends R360 000, closing equity R3 045 000. Calculate ROSHE, ROTCE, EPS, DPS, the pay-out rate and NAV, and state the question each answers.
questions.expected_answer: ROSHE: R450 000 divided by R3 000 000 is 15 percent — what the shareholders' own money earned after tax. ROTCE: R620 000 plus R80 000 gives R700 000, divided by R4 000 000 is 17,5 percent — what the whole pot of long-term capital earned before the funders divided it, which is why interest and tax are added back. EPS: R450 000 over one million shares is 45 cents — what each share earned. DPS: R360 000 over one million is 36 cents — what each share was actually paid. Pay-out rate: 36 over 45 is 80 percent — four-fifths distributed, one-fifth retained. NAV: R3 045 000 over one million is 304,5 cents — what each share is worth according to the books, assets minus liabilities per share. Each numerator must contain exactly the income belonging to the capital in its denominator: shareholders' profit over shareholders' capital, total return over total capital.

questions.question: Using ROTCE of 17,5 percent, an interest rate of about 8 percent on loans, a debt-equity ratio of 0,31 to 1, and a share price of 380 cents against NAV of 304,5 cents, advise Khanya's directors on further borrowing and interpret the share price.
questions.expected_answer: The gearing argument: every borrowed rand earns 17,5 cents through the business while costing about 8 cents in interest — positive gearing, with the difference accruing to shareholders. At 0,31 to 1 the company is lightly geared, so there is room to borrow for expansion, and doing so should lift ROSHE. The caution that earns the balancing mark: interest is a fixed charge owed in bad years too, so gearing amplifies both directions, and the argument dies if returns fall toward the cost of debt. The share price: the market pays 75,5 cents per share above the book value of the net assets. That premium is the market pricing what the balance sheet cannot record — expected future profits, customer loyalty and management quality — and it signals confidence in the company. A price far below NAV would signal expected decline, or an opportunity for a buyer acquiring assets at a discount; either reading is acceptable if argued. The discipline throughout: quote the figure, compare it to something, judge with a reason.

questions.question: Describe the main sections of a published annual report and explain how a reader should use each, including the King Code and the ethics of share-price manipulation.
questions.expected_answer: The directors' report is the board's own account of the year — operations, dividends, significant events — informative but written by the players about their own match, so it is read critically. The independent auditor's report is read first: an unqualified opinion means the statements fairly present the position; a qualified opinion means fair except for listed matters; a disclaimer or adverse opinion undermines the statements entirely, and any ratios built on affected figures inherit the doubt. The abridged financial statements carry the figures for analysis using the full toolkit. The governance section discloses directors' remuneration, board committees and compliance with the King Code, which demands responsibility, accountability, fairness and transparency — and remuneration should be read against performance, since pay rising while earnings per share falls is a legitimate shareholder challenge at the annual general meeting. The ethics thread: spreading false information to move the share price and trading on inside knowledge the market lacks are both illegal forms of share-price manipulation, and scenarios about directors buying or selling before results are announced test exactly this. An unqualified audit opinion certifies fair presentation, not good management — the other sections answer the questions the audit never asked.
